{{Short description|On transcendence of certain numbers}}
'''Hilbert's seventh problem''' is one of [[David Hilbert]]'s [[Hilbert problems|list of open mathematical problems]] posed in 1900. It concerns the [[irrational number|irrationality]] and [[transcendental number|transcendence]] of certain numbers.{{r|hilbert}}

== Background and the statement ==
In 1919, Hilbert gave a lecture on [[number theory]] and spoke of three conjectures: the [[Riemann hypothesis]], [[Fermat's Last Theorem]], and the transcendence of <math> 2^\sqrt{2} </math>. He mentioned to the audience that he did not expect anyone in the hall to live long enough to see proof of this result.{{cn|date=January 2026}} In his seventh problem, under the title "Irrationality and Transcendence of Certain Numbers" (''Irrationalität und Transzendenz bestimmter Zahlen'' in German),{{r|hilbert}} two specific equivalent questions were asked:{{r|fn}}
#In an [[isosceles triangle]], if the ratio of the base [[angle]] to the angle at the vertex is [[algebraic number|algebraic]] but [[irrational number|not rational]], is the ratio between base and side always [[transcendental number|transcendental]]?
#Is <math>a^b</math> always transcendental, for algebraic <math>a \not\in \{0,1\}</math> and irrational algebraic <math>b</math>?
For preliminary, an algebraic number is the [[Root of a function|root]] of a non-zero polynomial in one variable with [[Rational number|rational coefficients]], and a transcendental number is the opposite of an algebraic number (i.e., not the root of a polynomial). An irrational number is a number that cannot be expressed by the [[fraction]] of two integers; the denominator cannot be zero.

In addressing the second question more specifically, Hilbert asked about the transcendence and irrationality of the numbers <math> 2^\sqrt{2} </math> and <math> e^\pi = i^{-2i} </math>. The first number is known as the [[Gelfond–Schneider constant]] or the Hilbert number.{{r|hilbert}}

==Solution==
{{main|Gelfond–Schneider theorem}}
The proof regarding the transcendence of <math> 2^\sqrt{2} </math> was published by Kuzmin in 1930, well within [[David Hilbert|Hilbert]]'s own lifetime. Namely, Kuzmin proved the case where the exponent <math> b </math> is a real [[quadratic irrational]].{{r|kuzmin}}

In 1934, [[Aleksandr Gelfond]] and [[Theodor Schneider]] proved more generally, by extending the number <math> b </math> to an arbitrary algebraic irrational. Respectively, they independently answered the second problem in the affirmative and refined it. This result is known as Gelfond's theorem or the [[Gelfond–Schneider theorem]].{{r|gelfond|schneider}} From the generalization's point of view, this is the case
<math display="block"> b \ln{\alpha} + \ln{\beta} = 0</math>
of the general linear form in logarithms, which was studied by Gelfond{{cn|date=January 2026}} and then solved by [[Alan Baker (mathematician)|Alan Baker]],{{r|baker}} who was awarded a [[Fields Medal]] in 1970 for this achievement. The result is called the Gelfond conjecture or [[Baker's theorem]].
